title: Christie Blatchford: Officer who shot and killed mentally ill man was reasonably in fear for his life and out of options
subtitle: Michael Eligon was advancing in markedly determined fashion upon police, with two pairs of scissors, when he was shot and killed
article: At the most, from the time Toronto Police Constable Louie Cerqua got out of his squad car until he fired three times at Michael Eligon, one whole minute had elapsed.
By my reckoning, it was more like 30 seconds, tops.

The young officer spent 68.5 times that long Monday answering questions about the incident - where he stepped and where he didn\'t, what use-of-force options he considered and which he didn\'t, and why not, whether there was any wind that day, and what Mr. Eligon might have been thinking, and what tone of voice he used when he said, "One of you is going to die."
Such is the nature of hindsight, of course, indeed of the coroner\'s inquest itself: Objects in the mirror then were closer, and moving a hell of a lot faster too, than may appear now.

Const. Cerqua was testifying at the inquest examining the Toronto Police shooting deaths of three people - Mr. Eligon, who was 29 when he was fatally injured on Feb. 3, 2012; Sylvia Klibingaitis, 52, who died on Oct. 7, 2011; and Reyal Jardine-Douglas, who was 25 when he died on Aug. 29, 2010.

All three were suffering some sort of mental health crisis at the time of their deaths and all were armed with edged weapons, in Mr. Eligon\'s case two pairs of scissors. All were, as videos clearly show, advancing in what can collectively be described as markedly determined fashion upon the officers.

(In fairness, in Ms. Klibingaitis\'s case, she sprinted at police, a huge knife in her hand, like a creature out of a certain Anthony Perkins\' horror film whose name likely would be deemed insensitive to mention here.)
But in the three incidents, by any objective measure, the officers who fired were reasonably in fear for their lives and out of options.
But never mind any of that nonsense!

Inquests are always about coming up with recommendations to prevent similar deaths in the future, which means they are necessarily about, as Const. Cerqua put it once, explaining "when I should have zigged instead of zagged."

Thus the fabulous role-play Monday, wherein Peter Rosenthal, the lawyer for Mr. Eligon\'s family and a lovely gentlemen of a certain age, tried to get Const. Cerqua to imagine him with a pair of scissors in each hand.
"I\'m going to continue to retreat so you stop me where you would feel safe," Mr. Rosenthal said.
Const. Cerqua gently pointed out Mr. Eligon\'s pace, age and, more important, his actions earlier that morning made for a wholly different situation.
Mr. Eligon had been taken to Toronto East General Hospital by other officers.

There, after 36 hours with no treatment and only a blue hospital gown to show for his efforts, he had walked out of the joint, marched to a nearby convenience store, stole the scissors and, when the shopkeeper politely attempted to dissuade him, promptly stabbed him in the hand.
Thus armed, clad only in his gown, black socks and a toque, Mr. Eligon then tried to carjack a woman and was prowling the east end neighbourhood, apparently looking for houses to break into.
The 911 switchboard lit up with calls from alarmed residents; officers, responding to various hotshots on their radios, flooded the area.
One constable, Nick Alley, was actually flagged down by a resident.
The officers, most of them so young they might as well have been, as Const. Cerqua\'s lawyer, Gary Clewley, put it with trademark insouciance, "born an hour ago," converged upon Milverton Boulevard.
Mr. Eligon was spotted hopping a backyard fence, then running down a driveway, then emerging onto the street.

By the time Const. Cerqua\'s in-car camera picked up Mr. Eligon, the officers were scrambling backward, with Const. Alley, shouting at them to "Back up, back up!" and the rest shrieking at Mr. Eligon to drop his weapons.
This was the scenario Mr. Rosenthal was trying to re-enact. As he told Const. Cerqua once, "I have an edged weapon. You have a firearm pointed at my centre mass.
"I would put it to you, you should feel thoroughly safe," Mr. Rosenthal asked.
"I don\'t feel safe, period," Const. Cerqua said mildly.

"Tell me when you feel safe," Mr. Rosenthal said, still walking backward through the room, much further than the eight- to 10 feet that in real life separated the two men at the time Const. Cerqua fired, "where you feel confident enough" not to shoot.
Mr. Rosenthal asked if the officer had thought of saying, "\'Michael, can we help you?\'"
"It never crossed my mind," Const. Cerqua replied.

Mr. Rosenthal asked if he\'d considered using pepper spray. He asked if he had thought of using a parked truck as a barrier, to buy more time. He asked if his decision to shoot was influenced by an "undue fear" of edged weapons.

But it wasn\'t an undue fear. It was an entirely reasonable one: Mr. Eligon was close, getting closer; he was armed with scissors he had already used; he was unresponsive to the shouted commands to stop.
Const. Cerqua began his Toronto Police career in May of 2011. By the time he encountered Mr. Eligon, he had all of nine months on the job and was 26 years old.
Yet in the minutes before Mr. Eligon was spotted, he still had the presence of mind to park by a neighbourhood school, just in case he surfaced there.

In the same way, Const. Alley, when Mr. Eligon was on the street, dying - so narrow and slight a figure he looked deflated, almost flat - and it was almost over, had the composure to find the resident who had flagged him down.
He didn\'t want the man to feel guilty. He could see "the grief on his face", he said. He wanted to console him.
These are remarkably mature and capable young officers.
"I don\'t envy the position you guys are in," Const. Cerqua told a juror who asked what his recommendations might be.
"I don\'t envy yours either," the juror replied. Amen.
